He promised the king a box of gears that could predict eclipses, and the whole court laughed.
You see, picture a craftsman in a world where the sky belongs to the gods.
The king gave him one chance: be right, or lose your head.
The craftsman said nothing. He kept cutting gears.
Weeks later, he turned the crank. The dials said: forty days.
The court laughed harder. Nobody tells the Sun when to vanish.
Forty days later, at noon, the sky went dark.
But in 1901, sponge divers pulled a corroded lump of bronze from a Roman shipwreck.
X-rays looked inside: thirty bronze gears. One matched the 19-year cycle of the Moon. Another, the 223-month cycle of eclipses.
An eclipse calculator, over two thousand years old.
The sea kept his machine. History lost the man.
